item.title: October US ISM services 54.5 vs 54.8 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 54.9
  • Prices paid 73.0 vs 74.0 prior
  • New orders 55.9 vs 59.8 prior
  • Employment 51.4 vs 50.1 prior
  • Business activity 53.8 vs 56.5 prior

This is a step back from September and suggests there is no big acceleration ongoing in the US economy but that services are still strong. Prices paid are extremely elevated but ticked dow. There has been no dollar reaction to the report.

For background, the Institute for Supply Management’s Services PMI is one of the most closely watched monthly gauges of the US economy. It’s released at 10 am ET on the third business day of the month, two days after its manufacturing counterpart, and is based on a survey of purchasing and supply executives at services firms. The report was known as the non-manufacturing index until 2020.

Like other PMIs, it’s a diffusion index where readings above 50 signal expansion and below 50 signal contraction. The headline is a composite of four equally weighted sub-indexes: business activity, new orders, employment and supplier deliveries. Because services make up the bulk of US economic activity and employment, the survey is often seen as a better reflection of the broader economy than the manufacturing ISM.

The prices index is frequently the most market-moving part of the report. It measures the share of firms paying higher prices for inputs and has become a key early signal for services inflation, which the Federal Reserve watches closely. The employment index offers an early read on hiring, often scrutinized ahead of the monthly jobs report.

Other components include inventories, backlog of orders, new export orders, imports and inventory sentiment. The report also lists how many of 18 services industries reported growth and includes anonymous respondent comments on demand, costs, tariffs and policy, which are widely quoted.

ISM data generally carry more weight with markets than the S&P Global services PMI because of their longer history and larger following. A surprise in the headline or prices index can move Treasury yields, the US dollar and equities, particularly when the economy appears to be at a turning point.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The biggest loser of the US elections was data centers
item.description:
One of the clearest messages from Tuesday's US midterm elections had nothing to do with Republicans or Democrats. It was a resounding rejection of data centers.

Communities across the country voted on dozens of ballot measures involving data-center construction, zoning, moratoriums and development restrictions. Almost everywhere, voters came down on the same side: against new development.

The margins were extraordinary in many places.

  • Granville, Ohio: 82.5% voted to prohibit data centers.

  • Sunbury, Ohio: 78.6% supported a ban on large data centers, potentially affecting a proposed $2 billion Amazon project.

  • Trenton, Ohio: 79.6% backed restrictions on large-scale data centers.

  • Edgewater, Florida: 77.6% supported a ban on new data centers and expansions.

  • Bloomington, Illinois: 77.6% supported an advisory moratorium.

  • Alhambra, California: 82.4% supported a ban, with counting still incomplete.

  • Boulder City, Nevada: 70.6% opposed allowing data centers in a designated development area.

  • Ashville, Ohio: 81.6% rejected a development agreement involving EdgeConneX.

  • Downe Township, New Jersey: 87.3% opposed data-center development in an advisory vote.

In Illinois, four Madison County townships voted on whether officials should permit data centers. All four rejected the idea, with opposition ranging from roughly 74% to 83%.

The results weren't literally unanimous. One North Dakota measure reportedly went the other way, and several jurisdictions were still counting. But the overall picture is remarkable, and looks like it will be 44 of 45 ballots rejecting data centers and many pro-data center candidates losing elsewhere. This is a 70/30 issue, if not 80/20.

You would think they were putting toxic waste on the agenda.

The consistency of the results is difficult to ignore.

The opposition also cuts across party lines and geography. The complaints are familiar: electricity costs, water consumption, noise, pressure on local infrastructure and concerns that large technology companies receive tax incentives without delivering enough permanent employment.

For financial markets, this is worth watching closely. Shares of Neoclouds NBIS (-4.8%) and CRWV (-6.5%) are down heavily today despite a big rebound in stock futures that has the S&P 500 up 1.1%.

The AI investment boom depends on an enormous pipeline of new data centers, along with the power generation and transmission capacity needed to run them. Technology companies have committed extraordinary amounts of capital to this buildout, and those spending plans underpin expectations for semiconductor demand, electrical equipment, utilities and construction.

Tuesday's votes won't bring that investment to a halt. Local bans can face legal challenges, and developers can shift projects to more accommodating jurisdictions. Some measures are also nonbinding.

The industry has generally focused on whether enough chips, electricity and capital are available to support its expansion. The election results suggest obtaining permission to build may become just as important and I think there is already a shift underway where tech companies are forced to buy that consent via expensive taxes or paying for things like schools. That's flipped the old script of companies getting tax waivers to build in communities.

There is also a political dimension. With voters delivering lopsided verdicts against data centers, politicians at the state and federal levels may find it increasingly attractive to promise restrictions, tougher permitting rules or greater protection against electricity-price increases. I think that flows towards AI in general, if not tech.

The irony is that the United States is pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into winning the AI race, but voters in the communities being asked to host the infrastructure increasingly want no part of it.

Nasdaq futures are up 0.4% today.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: How Congressional control shapes US fiscal policy and financial markets
item.description:
US elections can have a significant impact on financial markets, not only because they determine who controls the government but also because they influence expectations about future fiscal policy. One of the most important aspects of the US political system is that Congress controls the government's spending and taxation decisions, giving election outcomes the potential to reshape the economic outlook.

When one party controls both chambers of Congress, passing legislation can become easier. Conversely, divided government, where different parties control the presidency, the House and/or the Senate, can create political gridlock and make major fiscal changes more difficult. These political dynamics matter because fiscal policy influences economic growth, inflation, government borrowing and, ultimately, the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

How congress controls fiscal policy

The US Congress plays a central role in determining fiscal policy through three main channels: government spending, taxation and borrowing. It approves federal spending through appropriations legislation, determining how much money is allocated to areas such as defence, infrastructure, healthcare and social programmes. The President can propose a budget, but Congress ultimately decides what spending legislation to pass.

Congress also determines federal tax policy. Changes to corporate taxes, personal income taxes and other forms of taxation can influence household consumption, business investment and government revenues. Tax legislation must pass both chambers before being sent to the President.

When federal spending exceeds tax revenues, the government runs a budget deficit and needs to borrow to finance the difference. Congress authorises borrowing and controls the statutory debt ceiling, while the Treasury manages the issuance of government securities. These three channels are closely interconnected. Higher government spending or lower taxes generally increase the fiscal deficit unless offset by other measures, while spending cuts or tax increases can reduce borrowing requirements.

Why divided government can limit fiscal expansion

When the President's party does not control both chambers of Congress, passing major fiscal legislation becomes more difficult. For example, a Republican President seeking additional tax cuts or higher defence spending may struggle to secure approval from a Democratic-controlled Congress. The opposition can block legislation, demand concessions or negotiate changes that reduce the overall fiscal impact.

This can create a more restrictive fiscal environment, with fewer opportunities for large spending packages or additional tax cuts. However, divided government does not automatically mean fiscal contraction. Congress can still reach bipartisan agreements, particularly on politically important areas such as defence spending, infrastructure and disaster relief. Existing spending programmes also continue unless legislation changes them.

Congressional control, however, does not give Congress complete control over the President's foreign or trade policy. The President retains significant executive authority over tariffs and military operations, although Congress has important constitutional powers over trade regulation, declarations of war and government funding. A divided Congress can constrain domestic fiscal expansion without necessarily preventing the administration from pursuing its broader geopolitical or trade agenda.

How congressional control influences financial markets

The implications for financial markets depend on how traders interpret the resulting fiscal outlook. The same political outcome can affect different asset classes in different ways.

Treasury yields

Government borrowing is one of the most direct channels through which fiscal policy affects bond markets. More fiscal expansion generally means higher government spending, larger deficits and potentially greater Treasury issuance. If markets expect increased borrowing, they may demand higher yields to absorb the additional supply of government debt. Fiscal expansion can also support economic growth and increase inflationary pressures, potentially pushing real and nominal yields higher. 

Conversely, expectations of fiscal restraint can reduce projected borrowing requirements and inflationary pressures, creating room for Treasury yields to decline. However, if fiscal restraint is expected to weaken economic growth, markets may increase demand for government bonds, pushing yields lower even without a meaningful reduction in Treasury issuance.

The US dollar

The dollar is influenced by several factorsl like economic growth expectations, capital flows and risk sentiment. The most important, though, is interest rates expectations.

Fiscal expansion can support the dollar if it strengthens economic growth and pushes Treasury yields higher as Federal Reserve rate hikes become more probable. Fiscal restraint can have the opposite effects. Lower borrowing expectations and reduced inflation pressures may weigh on Treasury yields and interest rate expectations, making the dollar less attractive, especially at overstretched levels.

Equities

The impact on equities is more nuanced because different sectors respond differently to fiscal policy. If we look at the broader stock market, the impact is mainly on growth expectations. Fiscal expansion generally supports aggregate demand, benefiting companies through stronger consumption, investment and government contracts. Tax cuts can also increase corporate profitability by reducing the tax burden on businesses.

Conversely, fiscal restraint can weigh on economic growth and corporate earnings, particularly in sectors that depend heavily on government spending or domestic demand. However, lower Treasury yields can provide some support to equities by reducing the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings and making bonds relatively less attractive. This means that a politically driven decline in yields can support equity valuations even if the underlying fiscal outlook becomes less favourable.

Why markets react to expectations rather than actual policy changes

One of the most important concepts in trading is that financial markets are forward-looking. Traders do not wait for legislation to be passed before adjusting their positions. They continuously assess the probability of different political outcomes and incorporate those expectations into asset prices.

For example, if markets expect that a divided Congress will prevent additional tax cuts and spending increases, Treasury yields and the dollar may start declining before any fiscal legislation changes. 

Positioning also matters. If investors are heavily positioned for a particular political or economic outcome, even a relatively modest change in expectations can trigger significant price movements as those positions get unwound.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada Trade Balance ($C) for September +5.35B vs +4.1B estimate
item.description:
• Prior month +4.2B

The details of the Canada Trade Balance for the month of September:

  • Merchandise trade balance: C$5.4 billion surplus. Prior C$4.95 billion surplus 9revised from C$4.20B.

  • Exports: +0.2% MoM to C$78.6 billion vs C$78.41B prior. Prior +3.2%.

  • Imports: -0.3% MoM to C$73.71 Billion vs C$73.46B. Prior -2.2%.

  • Export volumes: -4.0% MoM.

  • Import volumes: -2.5% MoM.

  • Trade surplus with the United States: C$12.3 billion. Prior C$12.1 billion.

  • August exports revised to C$78.4 billion from C$77.9 billion; imports revised to C$73.5 billion from C$73.7 billion.

Canada’s merchandise trade surplus widened to C$5.4 billion in September from C$5.0 billion in August, according to Statistics Canada. Exports edged higher while imports declined, but the details were mixed. Oil and gold supported the headline export gain, while export volumes fell sharply.

Energy exports rose 8.2%, led by crude oil and bitumen, up 10.2%, largely because of higher prices. Metal and non-metallic mineral exports increased 8.6%, supported by gold. However, eight of 11 export categories declined. Excluding energy and metal and non-metallic mineral products, exports fell 5.6%.

On the import side, motor vehicles and parts fell 9.1%, following a 9.3% decline in August. That weakness was partly offset by a 29.4% jump in computer and peripheral imports, mainly reflecting processing units used in data centres coming from the United States.

Quick analysis: The surplus improved, but the export details take some shine off the headline. Higher commodity prices helped lift export receipts while volumes declined. Third-quarter export volumes also fell 0.6%, with import volumes down 1.6%. That gives the Bank of Canada a softer underlying activity signal than the nominal surplus alone suggests. A wider surplus would normally support the Canadian dollar and pressure USDCAD lower, but the broad export weakness could temper that support.

What this report measures: Canada’s monthly merchandise trade report tracks goods exported to and imported from other countries. A surplus means goods exports exceed imports. Traders watch both dollar values and inflation-adjusted volumes because higher prices can lift trade values without an increase in the quantity of goods shipped.

Source: Statistics Canada, November 4, 2026; international merchandise trade table.

The USDCAD is trading near session lows

The USDCAD is trading near session lows helped by the general trend to the downside in the greenback post the US election .  Technically, the price has extended below the swing area between 1.3936 up to 1.3963. It also fell below the 61.8% retracement at 1.39497.  The swing area is now a close risk area for traders. Stay below is more bearish. On the downside the 200 day MA at 1.38919 is the next key target to aspire toward. Move bwow that MA would ad to the bearish bias.   

On a break above teh 1.3963 level, we could see sellers shift back to buyers and look toward teh 50% retracement at 1.40162. Late yesterday, the price moved up to test that level only to find willing sellers.

item.title: US September international trade balance -105.0B vs -108.0B expected
item.description:
• Prior was -$105.6 billion
  • Goods trade balance -135.0B vs -$134.9 billion prelim
  • US-China balance -$21.87 vs -$18.4 prior
  • Exports $321.51 billion vs $315.67 billion prior

Imports of capital goods are a good measure of AI spending and that rose to $157.97 billion vs $146.41 billion previously. Expect that to stay high as long as the buildout continues.

For background, the US international trade report is published jointly by the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis at 8:30 am ET, about five weeks after the reference month ends. It provides the full picture of US trade, adding services and detailed breakdowns to the advance goods figures released a week or so earlier.

The headline figure is the overall trade balance in goods and services. The US runs a large deficit in goods, partly offset by a surplus in services such as travel, financial services, intellectual property charges and business services. The goods figures here are on a balance of payments basis, which adjusts the Census data for coverage and timing, so they differ slightly from the advance numbers.

The report breaks exports and imports down by end-use category and shows bilateral balances with major trading partners, including China, Mexico, Canada, the European Union, Japan and Vietnam. Those country figures have become politically charged, as bilateral deficits feature heavily in tariff policy and trade negotiations.

For GDP, the key detail is real goods trade, adjusted for inflation, which feeds into the net exports component. Revisions to the advance goods data and the addition of services can shift growth estimates.

Trade has been one of the most volatile areas of the US economy in recent years. Waves of tariff front-running, followed by pullbacks, have produced record swings in imports and the deficit. Large flows of nonmonetary gold have added further noise. The report rarely moves currencies on its own, but it’s central to tracking how tariffs are reshaping supply chains and trading relationships. Statistics Canada often releases its own monthly trade data at the same time.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar falls, stocks rise as Democrats take Congress
item.description:
The US dollar is lower, Treasury yields are falling and US stocks are trading higher as markets digest a major shift in Washington. Democrats have won control of both the House and Senate, setting up divided government for the final two years of President Trump’s term. The new Congress takes office in January.

For traders, the immediate question is how much of the initial reaction can hold. Lower yields and falling oil provide a more supportive backdrop for equity buyers, but the election result alone does not determine the next trend. Inflation, employment, earnings and the Fed remain key barometers.

A tougher legislative path in Washington

The result gives Democrats greater power to challenge the administration through congressional investigations, negotiations over legislation and Senate approval of presidential nominees. Trump retains his veto, leaving both sides facing limits on what they can deliver.

From a market perspective, additional tax cuts and major spending packages could face higher hurdles. That could temper expectations for further fiscal stimulus and help explain the focus on lower Treasury yields. However, divided government also creates the potential for confrontations over government funding and the debt ceiling.

Technology oversight is another area to watch, including artificial intelligence, data centers and cryptocurrencies. Greater scrutiny would not automatically translate into sweeping legislation. Traders need to distinguish between a change in the political backdrop and policy changes that actually become law.

Middle East: Diplomacy continues, but risks remain

The Middle East headlines continue to pull in both directions. Reports of concessions in US-Iran negotiations were followed by Iranian pushback that an agreement was close. As outlined in InvestingLive’s latest oil update, the diplomatic picture remains unsettled.

Qatar continues mediation efforts, although a senior Iranian official told Reuters that the two sides remained far apart. US officials also reported limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, while Trump said he was in no hurry to resume attacks.

Separately, Reuters reported that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claimed four tankers had struck mines near the Strait of Hormuz and that two other vessels had been seized. That remains an attributed Iranian claim, but it underscores the continuing risk to shipping.

Crude oil nevertheless failed to hold its earlier advance. The price reached $97.15 before reversing lower and is trading near the session lows around $94.50. Buyers had their shot on the upside. They could not sustain the move, leaving sellers with the stronger hand heading into the North American session.

The dollar is lower across the board

The dollar is weaker against every major currency. Its largest decline is against the New Zealand dollar, while its smallest decline is against the Japanese yen.

  • EURUSD: 1.1261, up 0.61%.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3488, up 0.57%.

The broad participation matters. This is a dollar move extending across the major pairs, with the yen participating to a lesser degree.

The practical lesson is to define risk before chasing. An extended range is not a reversal signal. Buyers and sellers still need a technical level to lean against, with risk defined and limited.

US stocks trade mixed

The latest indications show the Dow and the S&P higher, but the Nasdaq is trading in volatile fashion above and below unchanged in early NA trading:

  • Dow industrial average: up 884 points.

  • S&P 500: up 68 points.

Treasury yields move lower

Lower yields can offer support to equities and gold while weighing on the dollar. The next barometer is whether those declines hold as US economic data arrive.

European stocks join the advance

European government bond yields are also lower. Germany’s 10-year yield is near 3.318%, France’s near 4.884% and the UK’s near 5.216%.

Gold rallies; Bitcoin rebounds from its overnight low

Gold is trading near $4,043, up approximately 2.9%, while silver is near $52.10, up about 4.65%. Both are advancing alongside the weaker dollar and lower Treasury yields.

Bitcoin fell to an overnight low of $75,666 before recovering to around $78,184 in the supplied snapshot. That is a rebound of $2,518 from the low.

The recovery shows that sellers could not sustain the overnight pressure. Buyers now need to build on that rebound. Holding above the overnight low preserves the recovery attempt, but a durable bullish shift still requires progress through technical resistance.

The ISM report’s employment and prices components will be particularly useful barometers for growth and inflation. With yields already lower and currencies having completed more than a normal day’s range, a surprise could test whether the overnight moves have further room to extend.

item.description:
Details

  • Prior was +90K
  • Construction +13K vs +15K prior
  • Manufacturing -1K vs +17K prior
  • Natural resources and mining -8K vs -1K prior
  • Financial activities +15K vs -16K prior
  • Professional and business services -27K vs -11K prior
  • Education and health services +28K vs +55K prior
  • Leisure and hospitality +19K vs +22K prior
  • Wages for all workers 4.7% vs +4.8% prior
  • Job stayers 4.4% vs 4.4% prior
  • Job changers 7.6% vs 7.3% prior

From the report, ADP chief economist Nela Richardson said:

"Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay. Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024."

For background, the ADP National Employment Report is a monthly estimate of US private-sector job growth produced by ADP Research in collaboration with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. It’s usually released at 8:15 am ET on the Wednesday before the government’s nonfarm payrolls report, giving markets an early, independent read on hiring.

The report is built from anonymized payroll data covering millions of workers at ADP’s client companies, one of the largest real-time samples of US employment. It covers private employers only, so it excludes government jobs. The headline figure is the monthly change in private employment, broken down by industry, establishment size and region.

ADP overhauled its methodology in 2022 to rely more directly on its own payroll records rather than modeling the government’s numbers. The report also includes pay insights, showing median annual pay growth for workers who stayed in their jobs and for those who changed jobs. The gap between the two is watched as a gauge of labor market tightness. ADP has also begun publishing weekly preliminary estimates, giving a higher-frequency read between monthly reports.

Despite the large sample, ADP has a mixed record as a predictor of nonfarm payrolls. The two measures use different methods and samples and can diverge sharply in any given month, with the differences often reversing over time. Traders tend to react to big surprises, but many economists treat ADP as one input among several rather than a reliable preview.

Its importance tends to rise when the official data are delayed or questioned, such as during government shutdowns, when it becomes one of the few timely reads on the job market.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

  • Bitcoin up 0.4% to $78,141

The US midterm elections went about as straightforward as it could. There were early signs that Democrats were going to pull off a complete sweep and it didn't take long before markets took that narrative and it played out without a hitch whatsoever.

They won both chambers of Congress, delivering a blow to the Republican governane in Washington. US president Trump tried to play things down by saying that he "could collaborate with Democrats on many issues" but resigned to defeat in saying that he will "accept the election outcome".

The initial market reaction was a wave of dollar selling alongside a rout in tech shares. The latter was the interesting bit as it tied to the fervently anti-AI and anti-data centre campaigning going into the midterms. As such, Nasdaq futures fell by over 2% earlier in the day.

But as we slowly progressed through European trading, US futures slowly pared losses and completed a stunning turnaround ahead of the Wall Street open later. S&P 500 futures are now up 1.0% with Nasdaq futures up by 0.4% on the day. What a comeback.

The dollar wasn't able to mirror that form though, as it struggled through the session. EUR/USD is up 0.6% to 1.1260 with AUD/USD also climbing by 0.6% to 0.7010 on the day.

With the greenback keeping weaker, gold took full advantage as the precious metal climbed by 3% to hang around $4,030-40 levels for the most part during the session. That comes amid the better risk mood with European shares also pushing solid gains and oil prices also easing off, with the bond market keeping more to the sidelines today.

For now, all eyes will be on whether Wall Street can maintain the optimistic turn in equities from European trading. If that fails to hold, I fear we could return back to the agenda from before the midterms. That being markets focusing back on AI worries with inflation fears also moving back into the spotlight.

In that lieu, a lot will hinge on what Trump decides to do next on the war against Iran. Will he take the election setback as a reason to pursue a diplomatic resolution? Or will he double down on military action? How that plays out will have very different consequences for markets. So, keep your eyes out on that if anything else.

item.title: AUD/USD rebounds above 0.7000 as US dollar slides but key technical hurdles remain
item.description:
Just when it looked like the aussie might be ready to throw in the towel this week, the dollar comes along to offer a helping hand. Talk about good timing, eh?

AUD/USD is bouncing back above the 0.7000 mark today, with the pair now trading around 0.7010 as the dollar comes under pressure following the US midterm elections. The rebound we're seeing is helping to undo the attempted downside break below the figure level after the RBA decision yesterday. However, I wouldn't get too carried away just yet.

Looking at the hourly chart, the latest push higher is running into resistance around 0.7020 from the 200-hour moving average (blue line). That remains the first hurdle for buyers to clear before attempting any stronger recovery.

And even then, the daily chart isn't exactly rolling out the red carpet either.

The 100-day (red line) and 200-day (blue line) moving averages, sitting in between 0.7030 and 0.7056, are still keeping a lid on any further upside momentum. And until buyers can break through those levels, I'd argue that the broader technical picture remains rather unconvincing at this stage.

It doesn't help that the RBA isn't offering much encouragement as well. Despite raising the cash rate to 4.85% (its highest in 18 years), the 6-3 split vote and Bullock's suggestion that policymakers should take stock of previous tightening have dampened expectations of further rate hikes.

As such, that leaves the dollar side of the equation to do most of the heavy lifting. And in looking at that, the key question now is what changes after the US midterms?

Well, let's start with what a Democratic sweep might mean for markets. The result is essentially throwing a spanner into Trump's policy agenda, with markets now weighing the prospects of greater political gridlock and tougher scrutiny of AI investment and data centre expansion. However, I think the bigger wildcard is what happens with the US-Iran war.

The question now is does Trump take the election setback as a reason to pursue a diplomatic resolution? Or does he double down on military action?

If Trump opts for the latter, that means we will see renewed escalation and heightened geopolitical tensions take over again. That will mean higher oil prices, which will then revive inflation concerns. And that will potentially keep Treasury yields elevated and trigger another flight to safety. In that scenario, the dollar could find renewed support while the aussie gets caught in another risk-off beatdown.

But if we do see Trump take a step back, then oil prices could retreat further and that will help ease inflation pressures as well as lift broader risk sentiment. That would be a welcome combination for the aussie, especially if lower inflation expectations also drag Treasury yields and the dollar down.

But with the US and Iran still far apart on key demands, I would be remiss not to point out that neither outcome should be taken for granted.

For now, I see the AUD/USD move today as a dollar-driven rebound more so than a convincing aussie comeback. And the bottom line is that until the moving averages give way on the charts on both the near-term and the daily timeframe, then buyers still have plenty of work to do to really convince of a renewed leg higher in the currency pair.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: FXStreet surpasses one million YouTube views in less than two months
item.description:
Barcelona, Spain, November 4th:FXStreet has surpassed 1 million views on its YouTube channel in less than two months, representing year-over-year growth of more than 1,500%, compared to the 61,000 views recorded during the same period last year. This milestone highlights the success of its video content strategy and reinforces the company's efforts to diversify its audience. During this period, the channel has accumulated nearly 40,000 watch hours, five million impressions, and more than 9,000 new subscribers, bringing its total subscriber base to over 146,000.

FXStreet's video content initiative has become one of the company's strategic pillars over the past year. Its goal is to expand the reach of its content and connect with new audiences, shifting from a model in which users actively seek information on FXStreet to one where the company distributes its content across the platforms traders already use.

The sustained growth in recent months supports the strategy led by Javier Hertfelder, Co-CEO of FXStreet and head of the project:

"Just over a year ago, we had a YouTube channel with around 120,000 subscribers and enormous untapped potential. Today, video has become a fundamental part of our strategy. The way people consume financial information is changing, and as a media company, we need to adapt. We can no longer simply wait for users to visit our website. We need to be present on the platforms where they search for information, learn, and engage."

Educational Content At The Heart Of Its Success

FXStreet's commitment to educational content that combines practical trading knowledge with analysis of current financial developments is one of the main pillars of its video strategy. The channel's programming focuses on technical analysis, macroeconomic insights, and live coverage of major events affecting financial markets.

Technical analysis accounts for a significant share of the channel's content. Ian Coleman, Senior Analyst at FXStreet, draws on nearly 40 years of trading experience to provide viewers with insights into topics such as supply and demand, chart patterns, and the fundamental concepts needed to get started in financial markets.

Meanwhile, Dhwani Mehta, Senior Analyst at FXStreet, covers macroeconomic developments of particular relevance to traders. Central bank interest rate decisions, inflation data, US Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP), and political events, such as the US midterm elections, are among the recurring topics featured on the channel. Mehta also specializes in commodities analysis, with a particular focus on Gold.

Finally, live coverage of major economic events allows traders to interact with analysts in real time, helping build an engaged trading community and encouraging two-way communication with viewers.

Video Content As A Response To Changing Consumption Habits

FXStreet's investment in video content reflects the need to diversify its audience sources and adapt to changes in how users search for and consume financial information.

The rise of generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models (LLMs), constant changes to Google's algorithms, and evolving content consumption habits are transforming how digital media companies reach their audiences.

Against this backdrop, the development of FXStreet's YouTube channel is part of a broader strategy to reduce reliance on traditional traffic acquisition channels and strengthen the company's presence on platforms where users regularly consume content.

Surpassing 1 million views in less than two months marks another milestone in FXStreet's digital transformation, as the company seeks to establish video as one of its primary content distribution channels and strengthen its direct connection with a global audience of traders.

About FXStreet

Founded in 2000, FXStreet is a leading financial media company focused on the global currency and financial markets. FXStreet provides market news, analysis, data, educational content and tools to traders and investors around the world, with a focus on independent, transparent and data-driven financial information.

item.title: How will central banks wrap up the year?
item.description:
The Fed, the ECB, and the Bank of Japan all kept rates on hold last week, just as expected. December is unlikely to bring any surprises either: unless the Middle East crisis eases, the base case is a rate hike, except perhaps in Japan, where the huge debt burden leaves little room for tightening. 

But why not act now?

Starting with the Fed, the case for a hike is already pretty compelling: inflation remains stubbornly high, hitting 3.6% year on year in September, while US growth is strong (GDP expanded at a 3.4% annualized rate in Q3 2026, up from 2.2% in Q2) and consumer spending and investment remain resilient. 

Hence, two FOMC members voted for a 25-basis-point hike. 

The rest of the committee, however, are holding back, apparently wary of what comes next in the Middle East: whether peace talks gain traction or tensions flare up again. Oil prices remain a key variable here: any renewed disruption to supply routes or energy infrastructure could push crude higher, adding to inflationary pressures and making a rate hike harder to avoid.

And even though Washington has signed off on a draft deal with Iran, covering mutual concessions on its nuclear program and frozen assets, there’s still no clear breakthrough in sight. 

As for the ECB, unlike in the US, consumption remains weak, there’s no AI investment boom, and inflation is largely driven by energy costs, so it too chose to wait and see how the situation in the Middle East unfolds. 

Finally, the Bank of Japan warned of fresh inflationary pressures from energy prices, a weaker yen, wage growth, and global demand for semiconductors and other AI-related products, thereby increasing the odds of further rate hikes. USDJPYis one of the key currency pairs to watch, as further yen weakness could fuel imported inflation and strengthen the case for monetary tightening. The risk is that this could unsettle global markets, triggering renewed volatility in currencies as the yen carry trade unwinds, as well as in bond markets. 

Where does that leave us? 

If the conflict escalates beyond sporadic exchanges of fire into full-scale military action, with fresh strikes on oil refineries and attempts to shut down the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, inflation could take another hit, leaving central banks with little choice but to act. 

An easing of tensions, on the other hand, could give central banks some breathing room, allowing them to keep rates on hold, or even start cutting. For now, though, markets are still bracing for tighter monetary policy, keeping pressure on stocks, bonds and even gold. 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: Eurozone inflation hits 4% for first time since 2023, piling pressure on ECB
item.description:
• Eurozone October preliminary CPI +4.0% vs +4.0% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.8%
  • Eurozone October preliminary core CPI +2.5% vs +2.5% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.5%

Headline annual inflation in the euro area climbs to 4% in October, hitting that mark for the first time since September 2023. Now, that's a doozy for ECB policymakers.

The culprit is once again higher energy prices, with energy inflation accelerating to 20.8% in October this year compared to the same month last year. Even on a monthly basis, energy prices were seen pushing up significantly in rising by 1.4%.

That being said, there were broad increases across all monthly estimates as headline prices went up by 0.4% on the month in October. The breakdown shows food prices being up 0.4% on the month and services also up 0.2% on the month.

The only good news is that core annual inflation is seen holding steady at 2.5% in October. That is unchanged from the previous month but it doesn't mean that the ECB can rest on its laurels. Services inflation remains stubborn and is seen rising to 3.3% annually, up from 3.2% in the previous month.

As such, that will continue to keep the pressure on policymakers as inflation pressures threaten to spill over more broadly. And the bigger the jump in energy prices and the longer it holds, the greater the risk of that spreading to broader categories. In turn, that will also increase the risks of second-round effects to the inflation outlook.

So, the ECB definitely has to be watchful here as they will be up against a tough balancing act amid slowing growth momentum especially in France. That threatens stagflation risks as well, which will be a much hotter topic come next year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq futures slide after Trump's midterm setback. AMD and Arista are telling a different story.
item.description:
Wall Street is confronting the prospect of tougher AI regulation after Democrats won control of Congress. Yet AMD and Arista Networks have attracted strong buying after earnings. Is this an early sign that investors are becoming more willing to reward strong corporate results?

Nasdaq futures initially fell sharply on Wednesday, November 4, following a sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections. Investors are reassessing the outlook for AI infrastructure, technology stocks and President Donald Trump's economic agenda.

But something interesting is happening beneath the market weakness.

AMD and Arista Networks are delivering a different message through their earnings reactions. Both attracted substantial buying after reporting results on Tuesday evening, despite a cautious broader market.

For traders and investors wondering what to do next, the distinction matters. A strong earnings season and a strong stock market are not necessarily the same thing. And the first signs of improving sentiment can sometimes appear in individual stocks before they spread to the wider market.

The question is whether we are beginning to see that change or merely two unusually resilient companies.

Why the midterm election result initially rattled Nasdaq futures

Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, delivering a significant political setback to Trump and the Republican Party.

The immediate concern for technology investors was not simply divided government. It was the possibility of greater scrutiny of AI investment, particularly the enormous infrastructure spending required to build data centres.

Restrictions involving electricity consumption, water usage, environmental requirements and construction approvals could complicate expansion plans, especially where Democrats gained influence at the state level. However, political proposals are not the same as enacted restrictions, and Trump retains presidential veto power.

As investingLive reported in its early coverage of the US futures selloff, Nasdaq futures were particularly vulnerable to concerns about the AI investment cycle.

At one stage, Nasdaq futures were down more than 2%. Yet the reaction was already evolving.

Our subsequent report showed US futures trimming their earlier losses, with Nasdaq futures recovering to around 0.4% below their previous reference level.

That recovery does not automatically resolve the market's concerns, but it does illustrate something worth remembering: the initial reaction to political news does not necessarily determine how the market will finish trading.

AMD and Arista provide something the broader market has been missing

The difference between strong business results and a positive stock-market reaction has become particularly important during this earnings season.

Several widely followed companies, including Netflix, Tesla, Meta, Alphabet and Apple, have encountered disappointing initial market reactions or reversals of earlier gains. Their individual circumstances differ, but collectively they help explain why investors have become more selective.

Now two major AI-related companies are challenging that pattern.

AMD: Buyers respond to accelerating data-centre growth

AMD reported third-quarter revenue of approximately $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year earlier.

More importantly, its data-centre revenue surged 97% to approximately $8.5 billion. The company also projected fourth-quarter revenue of around $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.

Investors have a concrete business development to assess, rather than simply another optimistic AI narrative.

The initial share-price response was strong.

In the overnight snapshot from approximately 02:05 Eastern on November 4, AMD traded near $519.60, up approximately 7.4% from Tuesday's $483.90 regular-session close.

The stock had previously touched approximately $530.38 overnight, temporarily exceeding the options market's pre-earnings expected move of 7.68%.

An expected move reflects the approximate size of a price change implied by options pricing. Exceeding it can signal stronger-than-anticipated repricing, but it does not establish that a rally will continue.

The other interesting observation is relative strength.

At a comparable overnight snapshot, Nasdaq futures were slightly negative relative to their previous 4 p.m. Eastern reference, while AMD remained substantially above its previous closing price.

That divergence suggests AMD was attracting company-specific buying interest despite weaker sentiment toward the broader technology market.

The next test is whether AMD can retain a substantial portion of those gains during Wednesday's regular trading session.

Arista Networks: A second piece of evidence

Arista Networks strengthens the case that AMD's reaction was not entirely isolated.

Arista reported third-quarter revenue of approximately $3.66 billion, representing 58.5% year-over-year growth. Its fourth-quarter revenue outlook was $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion.

The initial earnings-reaction snapshot showed Arista shares gaining approximately 9.5%, modestly exceeding the options-implied expected move of about 9.2%.

That is significant because Arista provides networking technology used in major data-centre environments.

AMD and Arista occupy different parts of the AI infrastructure market. Both delivered strong business results, and both initially received favorable reactions from investors.

This does not prove that fears about AI infrastructure spending are exaggerated. It does suggest that investors are still prepared to distinguish between companies delivering strong operating performance and broader concerns about the sector.

The earnings mood is still cautious, but something may be changing

Here is where I think the analysis becomes particularly useful.

Our preliminary assessment of recent earnings reactions has been cautious. Some influential companies have struggled to sustain positive post-earnings moves, even when their underlying businesses continued growing.

The November 3 assessment remained defensive, but the latest AMD and Arista reactions offer a possible early improvement.

ILLUSTRATIVE EARNINGS MOOD | NOVEMBER 3, 2026

4/10

Cautious

Possible improvement

AMD

+7.4%

Nov. 4 overnight snapshot

ANET

+9.5%

Initial earnings reaction

Strong leadership, but broader confirmation is still missing.

The 4/10 assessment is illustrative and not a calibrated or backtested market indicator. Company reactions are provisional, not completed November 4 regular-session returns.

A preliminary comparison of the latest after-hours earnings group suggests that AMD and Arista account for more than the group's net positive, company-size-weighted reaction. Other reporting companies collectively offset part of their strength.

That is an important distinction.

Two influential companies performing strongly can improve the overall picture without demonstrating that earnings sentiment has broadly recovered.

A more convincing change would involve additional companies receiving favorable reactions, fewer large negative surprises and positive moves that survive subsequent trading sessions.

It is also worth distinguishing earnings sentiment from the direction of Nasdaq itself. Investors might become more willing to reward individual companies while still demanding lower valuations for the wider technology sector.

Both developments can happen simultaneously.

There are more moving parts than earnings and elections

The bond market and geopolitical developments are also important.

The Democratic victory has encouraged buying in gold and US Treasury bonds, with some investors anticipating greater legislative gridlock and changes in fiscal policy expectations. Our analysis of why the midterm results are supporting gold explores another side of this market reaction.

Bond yields deserve particular attention because they influence the valuation of growth companies.

When yields climb, investors may demand higher returns from stocks whose valuations depend heavily on future profits. That can pressure technology shares even when their underlying businesses are expanding.

It connects with a broader question explored in our Macro Pulse discussion of when good news for stocks becomes bad news for the bond market.

Geopolitical uncertainty adds another layer.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards have claimed that four tankers were destroyed by naval mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Those claims had not been independently confirmed in the available reporting.

If confirmed, disruption to shipping could put renewed upward pressure on oil prices, potentially complicating the inflation and interest-rate outlook.

For investors, this means even a genuine improvement in earnings reactions could face resistance from forces outside individual companies' control.

What should stock traders and investors watch next?

Rather than forcing an immediate bullish or bearish verdict, I would focus on three developments.

First, can AMD and Arista hold their gains?

The November 4 regular session will provide more meaningful information than the initial overnight reaction alone.

If buyers defend a substantial portion of the gains, that would strengthen the argument that these companies are attracting durable interest. If the rallies rapidly reverse, the apparent improvement becomes less convincing.

Second, does the improvement spread beyond two companies?

Watch how other major earnings reporters react, particularly within technology and AI infrastructure.

A few strong winners can temporarily support sentiment. A broader increase in positive reactions would offer better evidence that investors' willingness to take risk is improving.

Third, does Nasdaq confirm the change?

A sustained recovery in Nasdaq futures and broader technology participation would provide a more supportive backdrop. A failed rebound, especially alongside renewed pressure on AI-related shares, would suggest that the broader market is not yet ready to follow the earnings winners.

For existing shareholders, the distinction also matters. A positive earnings reaction is encouraging, but valuation, business fundamentals, portfolio concentration and investment horizon remain relevant. For shorter-term traders, patience may be preferable to chasing an overnight move before the regular session tests it.

Could this be the beginning of a turnaround?

Possibly. But the evidence is not sufficient to call it one yet.

AMD and Arista have delivered something investors have not always been willing to provide during this earnings season: a strong positive response to strong corporate results.

That deserves attention, particularly when Nasdaq futures are under pressure from political developments and uncertainty surrounding AI infrastructure.

My takeaway is that Wall Street's earnings mood may be starting to improve before the broader market itself looks particularly healthy.

The next few sessions should help determine whether these are merely two impressive exceptions or early evidence of a more meaningful change.

For now, I would watch the leaders, measure how widely that strength spreads and avoid assuming that the first market reaction to the midterm elections has already settled the debate.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Italy October services PMI 52.0 vs 51.5 expected
item.description:
• Prior 51.7
  • Composite PMI 50.8 vs 50.8 expected
  • Prior 51.0

Key findings:

  • Growth in activity back in line with trend, supported by stronger new business inflows
  • Business sentiment strongest since November last year
  • Input cost inflation surges to almost four-year high

Comment:

Eleanor Dennison, Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence:

"The Italian service sector maintained its steady path of growth in October, even signalling stronger inflows of new work. The headline reading was back in line with its average trend, having crept higher over the month. "Granular sub-sector data revealed the commercial & professional services segment was the only drag, with the consumer services and software & communication sectors recording fresh upturns. The financials & real estate segment continued to lead growth, despite softening again. "The main challenges facing Italian service companies were softness in export demand and the build-up of cost pressures, two factors that are highly exposed to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Panellists often reported paying more for fuel and energy-related products in their reports, pushing the overall reading for input price inflation to one of its highest since the 2022 energy crisis. Transportation firms are struggling in particular with respect to costs, having signalled one of the strongest increases on record."Keep in mind that the Italian PMIs are never a market-moving release despite Italy being the third largest economy in the Eurozone. They do provide more information about economic activity in the euro area, though. 

As it stands, economic growth remains resilient in the Eurozone and inflationary pressure continue to build amid elevated energy prices caused by the US-Iran war. Everything hinges on the war. The ECB cannot fix an oil supply problem, but it can dampen demand through higher interest rates. The problem is that at some point, higher interest rates and elevated energy prices start putting a strong downward pressure on the economy. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections is driving gold higher and what to watch next
item.description:
Gold has been rallying strongly this morning as a blue sweep in the US midterm elections became a reality.

As mentioned yesterday, a Democratic congress is going to restrict further tax cuts, defence spending and fiscal expansion in general. This is positive for gold because it’s going to limit the rise in Treasury yields and the US dollar on lower rate hike expectations.

It could also support gold in case Trump decides to escalate the war with Iran as inflation expectations would rise alongside weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment.

Looking ahead, we have the US NFP report on Friday but it’s unlikely to change much for the Fed unless we see a jump in wage growth or surprisingly weak data. The focus will likely remain on US-Iran negotiations, but at this point, it looks like both an escalation and a de-escalation would provide support gold.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) is approaching the major downward trendline. We can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to target a break below the major upward trendline. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the 4,700 level next, with the 4,500 level as the first target.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we now have a minor upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the buyers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting a break above the downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets and target a break below the major upward trendline.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor support zone around the 3,970 level. If we get a pullback, we can expect the buyers to step in around the support, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break to extend the pullback into the minor upward trendline next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Todaywe have the US ADP and the US ISM Services PMI. Tomorrow, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. On Friday, we conclude the week with the US NFP report and the University of Michigan Consumer sentiment survey.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.
